did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with the title “A Psalm of David” and a call for the “sons of God” to give the Lord glory and strength. The expression describes the recipients as figures understood to possess status or power, without specifying their identity.
In verses 1–2, the call “Give to the Lord” is repeated three times, emphasizing the demand to acknowledge the Lord’s glory and worship him “in the splendor of holiness.”

The divine voice is described as sounding over the waters: “over the waters” and “over many waters.” The same verse also says, “The God of glory thunders,” linking the voice with the power of thunder.
The phrase “the voice of the Lord” appears seven times throughout verses 3–9. This repetition creates a rhythm and emphasizes the voice’s activity in the natural world.
The voice of the Lord is described as breaking cedars, especially the “cedars of Lebanon”—trees presented in the psalm as symbols of strength and endurance.

Lebanon and Sirion are described as leaping “like a calf,” while their movement is also compared to that of a “young wild ox.” These images portray mighty nature trembling before the power of the voice.
In verse 7, the voice is described as “hewing out flames of fire”—a powerful image of a voice cutting through or splitting flames.

One verse gives two contrasting descriptions of the voice’s actions: it “makes the deer give birth” and “strips the forests bare.” In contrast to the upheaval in nature, it says, “In his temple all cry, ‘Glory!’”

The psalm recalls the flood and presents the Lord as seated and reigning even after it: “The Lord sits enthroned over the flood.” Immediately afterward, it emphasizes the everlasting nature of his reign: “The Lord sits enthroned as King forever.”
The psalm’s conclusion moves from a description of the Lord’s power in nature to a blessing for his people: the Lord gives “strength” and blesses his people “with peace.”
